questions.q: Explain the idea of the three orders in medieval European society.
answer: Medieval European society was imagined as being divided into three orders, or groups, each with its own role.

answer.text: The first order was the clergy, the priests and monks of the Catholic Church. They were believed to serve society through prayer and religion. The Church was very powerful, owning vast lands and collecting a tax called the tithe, a tenth of the produce of the peasants.
The second order was the nobility, the lords and knights. They held land, gave military protection, and controlled the peasants who lived and worked on their estates.
The third order was the peasantry, the great majority, who produced food for all. They included free peasants and serfs, who were bound to the land and owed labour and dues to their lords.

answer: This threefold division expressed how medieval people understood their society.

questions.q: What factors led to the decline of feudalism in Western Europe?
answer: Feudalism, which had shaped Europe for centuries, gradually declined due to several connected changes.

answer.text: From the eleventh century, towns grew and trade revived, giving rise to a class of merchants and townspeople who lived by money rather than land. This weakened the land-based feudal bonds.

Severe famines, and above all the Black Death, a terrible plague, killed a large part of the population. The shortage of labour that followed allowed surviving peasants to demand wages and freedom, undermining serfdom.
Powerful kings built centralised states with their own armies and officials, reducing the independent power of the feudal nobility.

answer: Together these forces brought feudalism to an end and opened the way to the modern age.
